title: The Street Corner
sceneText:
The one who walked off has come back.

Three of you standing at the corner outside the chancery. Nobody proposes going anywhere else and nobody says they are leaving. The sun is very low, and there is still one band of light on the wall across the street, drawing upward.

“Sold out?” Thierry asks.

You say you sold out.

“Last market of October.” He moves the bottle to his other hand. “Next one is the Kindling, and what gets sold then is different.”

When he says it, it does not occur to him that you may not be here. Or it does, and he does not say so.

“I am out and about every day, mind,” he says suddenly. “Not that it was my choice either.”

You ask what he means by that.

“Third son of a count.” He says it lightly, as though it were somebody else’s business. “By rights I should have gone into the army, or married somebody I did not know and moved a long way off. I did not want either road.”

“So I made the Duke laugh, at a hunt.” He opens a hand. “That is all. One post, and I earned it myself.”

Timothy has not spoken at all. Thierry turns to him.

“And you, Kessler. Three years now.”

“I was posted here,” Timothy says.

That is the whole of it. Nothing else.

Thierry waits a moment to see whether more is coming. It is not.

“Posted here.” Thierry repeats it. “So you spend every day working out when you get moved on.”

“The fifth year,” Timothy says. “Usually the fifth year.”

The band of light finishes drawing up off the wall. The corner goes dim.

Thierry moves the bottle from one hand to the other, and then looks at you.

“And you, Steward,” he says. “I earned mine. He was posted. You came of your own accord.”

“So why do you want to stay here?”

choices.text: It is only a contract. Thirty days, and then I go

effects.logEntry: You said it was only a thirty-day contract.

choices.resultText:
“Right,” Thierry says.

He does not ask again. Neither does Timothy.

They stand a while longer, and then Thierry says it is getting dark and to mind the road. They go off in opposite directions.

You stand at the corner a few seconds before you remember that your cart is still on the east side of the square.

effects.logEntry: You said you needed the work.

choices.resultText:
“There is work everywhere,” Thierry says.

There is nothing aggressive in it; it is only said in passing. But once that sentence is standing there, nobody picks it up.

Timothy glances at the light and says he should be getting back.

As the three of you separate, Thierry says “see you next month”. He probably knows himself that next month you may not be here.

choices.text: I … I want a standing of my own

effects.logEntry: At the street corner you said something you had not expected to say.

choices.resultText:
For several seconds after you say it, nobody speaks.

You hear what you said. You do not know why you said it in front of an inspector and a forester.

And then Thierry laughs.

Loudly, with an echo in the emptied street. He waves a hand while he laughs, meaning that he is not laughing at you.

“Kessler,” he says, catching his breath. “Did you hear that?”

“I heard it,” Timothy says.

He puts a hand inside his uniform and takes something out. A card, dark ground, with a pattern pressed into it. You cannot tell what plant it is.

“This one is the Crown Lands’,” he says.

He does not hand it to you. He holds it up for you to see for a few seconds, and puts it away.

“Three years I have been here. People still look twice when it comes out.”

He smooths the pocket flat.

“Everybody around here carries a Valewisp one. The sort with the maple leaf. Martha’s, Gregor’s, Vallant’s, all of them,” he says. “They are not looking twice on purpose. It is only that they do not see this one about.”

He pauses.

“It is not hard to stay in this country — well, it is not that easy either — what is hard is everything after staying.”

It is the longest stretch he has spoken all day, and the first time it has not been him reciting terms.

And then he goes back to reciting terms.

“On residence,” he says. “Renewal of a temporary permit requires the guarantor to sign again. It may be submitted within seven days of expiry, and residence remains valid while the application is under consideration; you do not become illegal by waiting for a result.”

“The first renewal is ninety days. After three consecutive renewals it becomes annual. At five years you may apply for long-term residence, and long-term residence is not nationality.” He stops for half a second. “Nationality requires eight years, and a recommendation out of a local jurisdiction.”

“Eight years,” Thierry says. “Then you will be busy.”

He has not finished.

“And there is a thing he left out.” He points a finger in Timothy’s direction. “When you apply you have to enter a duchy. What you get after eight years is not only Marigni’s papers. It has to be some particular duchy’s as well.”

“So you will have to choose.”

He starts counting them off.

“Ridgecrest: six months of winter, you go out and never see the sun, hard people, hard drink. The Flamincore lot talk like men quoting a price; everything gets reckoned up first. Luminveil is all scholars, still arguing through dinner. Stormgale is on the sea, and does not ask where you are from, or anything else.”

“The Crown Lands.” He shakes his head. “The Crown Lands are not a place to live a life.”

He has finished counting.

“So choose here,” he says, and taps a finger against the bottle.

Then he holds the bottle out. You take it. There is half of it left, and it is still warm.

“When people here ask where you are from, they are not checking up on you,” he says. “They actually want to know.”

They go off in opposite directions. A few steps on, Thierry looks back.

“Keep the bottle.”
